title: Mind the step
hook: as you watch for nails when walking, watch over your ruling mind (Enchiridion 38)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was prosōpon, a role. Take one beyond your powers and two parts suffer. Your line was the part that really was yours.

Walk barefoot across a garage floor and watch what happens to you. Nobody has to tell you to pay attention. Your eyes go to every step. Your weight hangs back for a beat before each foot lands, just in case there's a nail, a screw, a sharp bit of glass. You do it without thinking, because you know what a nail in the foot feels like. Section thirty-eight of the handbook takes that ordinary carefulness and points it somewhere new.
screen: `BAREFOOT ON A GARAGE FLOOR.` → `EVERY STEP WATCHED.` → `MIND THE STEP.`

segments.voice: Just as when you walk you take care not to step on a nail or twist your foot, Epictetus says, take care in the same way not to harm your ruling mind. If you watched for this in every action, you'd go about each one more safely. The Greek is hēgemonikon, the ruling part. It's related to hēgemōn, a leader or guide. For the Stoics, the hēgemonikon was the command center of a person, where impressions are received, judged, and given or refused assent. Chrysippus, one of the school's early heads, even placed it in the heart. Marcus Aurelius uses the word again and again in his private notebook. Notice how much care you already give the body without effort. You watch for nails, wipe up spills, check the stairs in the dark. Epictetus asks for the same easy care for the part of you that decides. What does a nail look like for the mind? A judgment made in a rush. A resentment you agree to without checking. An impression, he's rude, I'm a failure, it's ruined, accepted at face value. Each one is a small injury to the ruling part, and like a foot injury, it changes how you walk for a while afterward. The fix isn't fear. It's attention at the moment of stepping: a beat before agreeing to the thought, the way you hang back before your foot lands.
screen: `WATCH THE MIND AS YOU WATCH YOUR FEET.` · `HĒGEMONIKON: THE RULING PART.` · `WE ALREADY GUARD THE BODY.` · `A RUSHED JUDGMENT IS A NAIL.` · then, large: `MIND THE STEP.`

segments.voice: If you can stand, walk slowly, feeling heel, ball and toes, each step watched as if the floor had nails; if you're sitting, rest your feet flat and feel them press the floor. Either way, when a thought arrives, give it the same beat you give a step. Look before you agree.
Hēgemonikon. The Stoic word for the ruling part of the mind, where impressions are judged. Guard it, Epictetus says, as you guard your feet. Today's word.
Your line: a beat before agreeing. The ruling part deserves the care your feet already get. That's day three hundred seventy-three.

screen: `DAY 373 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE FOOT MEASURES THE SHOE.`

howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism use slow, attentive walking as a reminder to pause before accepting a judgment, guarding the mind as carefully as their footing.

notes: Enchiridion 38 paraphrased: as in walking you take care not to step on a nail or turn your foot, so take care not to hurt your ruling faculty; if we observe this in every act we shall undertake it more safely. Confirm.
Chrysippus located the hēgemonikon in the heart (Galen, PHP books 2–3). Confirm.
hēgemōn as root and the English 'hegemony': standard etymology; confirm.
Outline practice is a three-minute walk; the in-app sit offers walking if the listener can stand, or feeling the feet if seated.
